pos: n. (the evening meal; the chief meal of the day, taken at its close)
etymology: Old French souper, to sup. In the Authorized Version supper is the last meal of the day, and therefore the meal Scripture keeps choosing for its pictures of the end — the great supper of the invited, the supper at which the new testament was given, and the marriage supper of the Lamb.
biblical_def: The supper is the evening meal, and Scripture makes it the meal of endings and of welcome. Our Lord tells of “a certain man” who “made a great supper, and bade many” (Luk 14:16), and at supper time sent his servant to say, “Come; for all things are now ready” (Luk 14:17) — the gospel call in six words, addressed to men who had already been bidden and who now produced a field, five yoke of oxen and a wife as reasons. The parable ends with the most sobering sentence in the chapter: “none of those men which were bidden shall taste of my supper” (Luk 14:24). Earlier in the same chapter our Lord tells the host himself whom to invite: not friends, brethren, kinsmen and rich neighbours who will bid thee again, but the poor, the maimed, the lame, the blind (Luk 14:12-13). Hospitality without recompense is the shape of the kingdom. Then the Supper itself: “Likewise also the cup after supper, saying, This cup is the new testament in my blood, which is shed for you” (Luk 22:20). The passover meal ends and a new ordinance begins in the same room. John records the quieter details of that evening — the rising from supper, the laid-aside garments, the towel — and Bethany's supper before it, where “Martha served: but Lazarus was one of them that sat at the table with him” (Joh 12:2), a dead man eating.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines supper as the evening meal, the last regular meal of the day; and notes the Lord's supper as the sacrament of the eucharist, instituted at the last supper of Christ with his disciples.
webster_full: SUPPER, n. The evening meal. People who dine at noon call their evening meal supper; but people who dine at three, four, five or six o'clock, take little or no supper.
1. The Lord's supper, the sacrament of the eucharist; the communion.
SUP, v.i. To eat the evening meal.
BID, v.t. To invite; to call; as, to bid guests to a wedding.
scriptures: Then said he unto him, A certain man made a great supper, and bade many:
And sent his servant at supper time to say to them that were bidden, Come; for all things are now ready.
Likewise also the cup after supper, saying, This cup is the new testament in my blood, which is shed for you.
For I say unto you, That none of those men which were bidden shall taste of my supper.
corruption_summary: The invitation is preached without the refusal; Luke 14 ends with men who were bidden and never tasted.
corruption_paragraphs: The great supper is a favourite text for describing God's open welcome, and the welcome is genuinely open — the servant is sent to the streets and lanes, to the highways and hedges, and the house is filled. But the parable is told to men at a Pharisee's table and it ends in a sentence of exclusion pronounced by the host himself. The excuses that produce it are not scandals; they are a field, some oxen, a marriage — ordinary goods preferred to the summons. A gospel preached as invitation without the possibility of a final refusal has removed the very edge our Lord put on it.

The second thing to recover is the guest list of Luke 14:12-13. Our Lord tells a man giving a supper not to invite those who can return the favour. That single instruction cuts across the way most hospitality is actually arranged, in the church as much as out of it, where meals circulate among people of similar means who will reciprocate. The recompense promised is at the resurrection of the just, which means the arrangement only makes sense if the resurrection is real. Christian hospitality is an eschatological act or it is merely society.
roots_summary: Greek deipnon (G1173), the chief or evening meal; deipneo (G1172), to sup; kaleo (G2564), to call or bid.
roots_lines: Greek deipnon (G1173) — the principal meal of the day, taken toward evening; Luke 14:16, 1 Corinthians 11:20 (the Lord's supper), Revelation 19:9 (the marriage supper of the Lamb).
Greek deipneo (G1172) — to take the evening meal; Luke 22:20, Revelation 3:20, I will come in to him, and will sup with him.
Greek kaleo (G2564) — to call, to invite, to bid; the verb behind them that were bidden.
Greek kaine diatheke (G2537, G1242) — new testament, new covenant; Luke 22:20, the cup after supper.
Greek antapodoma (G468) — a recompence, a repayment; Luke 14:12, the return our Lord tells the host not to seek.
usage: “Come; for all things are now ready” — the call, at supper time.
“None of those men which were bidden shall taste of my supper” — the parable's last word.
“The cup after supper” — the passover ends, the ordinance begins.

pos: n. (the marriage feast; the celebration attending a marriage)
etymology: From Saxon weddian, to pledge or covenant — the same root as wed and wager. The old English word names the pledge before it names the party, which is exactly the biblical order: a covenant made, and then a feast.
biblical_def: In the Authorized Version wedding means the marriage feast, and it belongs almost entirely to one parable. A king “sent forth his servants to call them that were bidden to the wedding: and they would not come” (Mat 22:3). The refusal is not indifference only; some took his servants and slew them. So the king says, “The wedding is ready, but they which were bidden were not worthy” (Mat 22:8), and the servants gather from the highways “both bad and good: and the wedding was furnished with guests” (Mat 22:10). That phrase — both bad and good — is the gospel's indiscriminate call. But the parable does not end there, and the church has often stopped a verse too soon. “When the king came in to see the guests, he saw there a man which had not on a wedding garment” (Mat 22:11), and to the king's question the man “was speechless.” A man may come in off the highway and still be cast out, if he comes in his own clothes. The wedding garment is the imputed righteousness of Christ, provided by the host and refused by the presumptuous. Luke adds the two other uses: the servants who wait for their lord's return from the wedding, ready to open immediately (Luk 12:36), and the counsel not to take the highest room when bidden to a wedding (Luk 14:8).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines wedding as marriage, nuptials, the ceremony or festivities of a marriage; and notes that in Scripture it denotes the nuptial feast.
webster_full: WEDDING, n. Marriage; nuptials; the ceremony or the festivities attending a marriage.
1. In Scripture, the nuptial feast; as, the wedding was furnished with guests.
WED, v.t. To marry; to take for husband or for wife; from the Saxon weddian, to covenant or pledge.
NUPTIAL, a. Pertaining to marriage; done at a wedding; as nuptial rites.
scriptures: And when the king came in to see the guests, he saw there a man which had not on a wedding garment:
Mat 22:8
Then saith he to his servants, The wedding is ready, but they which were bidden were not worthy.
So those servants went out into the highways, and gathered together all as many as they found, both bad and good: and the wedding was furnished with guests.
And ye yourselves like unto men that wait for their lord, when he will return from the wedding; that when he cometh and knocketh, they may open unto him immediately.
corruption_summary: Marriage itself is now redefined at the root, and the wedding reduced to a personal celebration; Scripture makes it a covenant and a summons.
corruption_paragraphs: Two corruptions run together. The first is the redefinition of marriage away from the creational pattern — one man and one woman, covenanting before God for life (Gen 2:24; Mat 19:4-6) — into a contract of mutual affection terminable at will and open to any pairing. Scripture forecloses this at the beginning and our Lord forecloses it again by citing the beginning. The second is subtler and nearer to the church: the wedding recast as a personal celebration built around the couple's preferences, in which vows before God have become the decorative frame around a party. The old English word remembers better than we do — to wed is to pledge, and the feast exists because a covenant was cut.

The parable adds the warning the church most needs. The wedding was furnished with guests, bad and good, gathered off the highway, and one man was cast into outer darkness for wearing his own clothes to it. The garment was the host's to give. Every man who intends to enter the kingdom in the merit of his own life is that man, and the speechlessness is the point: at the last there will be nothing to say. Blessed are they which are called unto the marriage supper of the Lamb (Rev 19:9) — and the fine linen, clean and white, is granted, not brought.
roots_summary: Greek gamos (G1062), a wedding, marriage feast; enduma gamou (G1742), a wedding garment; kaleo (G2564), to bid.
roots_lines: Greek gamos (G1062) — marriage, wedding feast; Matthew 22:2-12, John 2:1-2 (the marriage in Cana), Revelation 19:7.
Greek enduma (G1742) — a garment, that which is put on; Matthew 22:11-12, the wedding garment the guest lacked.
Greek phimoo (G5392) — to muzzle, to put to silence; Matthew 22:12, he was speechless — literally, he was muzzled.
Greek numphios (G3566) — bridegroom; Matthew 25:1-13, the parable that follows this theme to its watchful end.
Hebrew chathan (H2860) — bridegroom, son-in-law; Psalm 19:5, Isaiah 61:10.
usage: “The wedding is ready, but they which were bidden were not worthy”.
“Both bad and good: and the wedding was furnished with guests”.
“Not having a wedding garment? And he was speechless” — the last silence.

pos: v. (bidden to a meal or feast; summoned as a guest)
etymology: Latin invitare, to bid or entertain. In the Authorized Version the word appears three times, and each occasion is a meal that turned out to be about something other than the meal.
biblical_def: Three invitations, and not one of them is simply dinner. Samuel had told the cook to reserve the shoulder before Saul ever arrived: “set it before thee, and eat: for unto this time hath it been kept for thee since I said, I have invited the people” (1Sa 9:24). A young man out looking for lost donkeys sat down to a portion prepared for him in advance by a prophet who already knew he would be king. Providence had set the table days earlier. The second is Absalom's: “after two full years, that Absalom had sheepshearers in Baalhazor… and Absalom invited all the king's sons” (2Sa 13:23), and the invitation was the machinery of Amnon's murder. Two years of civility, and a feast for a killing. The third is Haman's, and it is the most pitiable sentence in Esther: “Esther the queen did let no man come in with the king unto the banquet that she had prepared but myself; and to morrow am I invited unto her also with the king” (Est 5:12). He recites the honour to his friends on his way home to build a gallows, and the second banquet is where he is unmasked. An invitation in Scripture is a place already prepared, and the guest rarely knows for what: a crown, a murder, or a hanging.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines invite as to ask to an entertainment; to summon; to allure or draw to; and invited as bidden or requested to come.
webster_full: INVITE, v.t. To ask to an entertainment; as, to invite friends to dinner.
1. To request the company of a person; to solicit to come or go.
2. To allure; to draw to; to tempt to come.
INVITED, pp. Solicited to come or go; requested in civility or friendship; allured.
scriptures: And the cook took up the shoulder, and that which was upon it, and set it before Saul. And Samuel said, Behold that which is left! set it before thee, and eat: for unto this time hath it been kept for thee since I said, I have invited the people. So Saul did eat with Samuel that day.
And it came to pass after two full years, that Absalom had sheepshearers in Baalhazor, which is beside Ephraim: and Absalom invited all the king's sons.
Est 5:12
Haman said moreover, Yea, Esther the queen did let no man come in with the king unto the banquet that she had prepared but myself; and to morrow am I invited unto her also with the king.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The verb means today what it meant in 1611. The only drift worth noting is theological rather than lexical: the language of inviting Jesus into your heart is a modern idiom found nowhere in Scripture, which speaks instead of repenting, believing, and receiving Him — and which makes God the one who calls, not the one who waits to be called.

The principle to recover is that the table is set before the guest knows why. Samuel had reserved a portion for a king who did not yet know he was one; Haman recited his invitation with delight on the evening before his ruin. Providence prepares in advance, and the invitation reveals nothing of the purpose. That is a comfort and a warning in the same breath: the believer does not need to see the design to trust the Host, and the man riding high on his welcome should remember Haman, who was genuinely invited and genuinely doomed.
roots_summary: Hebrew qara' (H7121), to call, to invite; mishteh (H4960), a banquet, a drinking feast; Greek kaleo (G2564), to call.
roots_lines: Hebrew qara' (H7121) — to call, proclaim, invite; 1 Samuel 9:24, 2 Samuel 13:23.
Hebrew mishteh (H4960) — a feast, a banquet (literally a drinking); Esther 5:12, the banquet Esther prepared.
Hebrew gazaz (H1494) — to shear; the sheepshearing that furnished Absalom's occasion.
Greek kaleo (G2564) — to call, to bid to a feast; the New Testament word behind them that were bidden.
Greek kletos (G2822) — called, invited; Romans 1:6-7, Revelation 19:9, blessed are they which are called.
usage: “I have invited the people” — and the shoulder had been kept for Saul.
“Absalom invited all the king's sons” — after two full years.
“To morrow am I invited unto her also” — Haman, on the way to build a gallows.

pos: n. (one who eats; in Samson's riddle, the devourer)
etymology: From eat, Saxon etan. The Authorized Version uses the noun three times, and its range is the whole distance between a lion's carcase and a loaf of bread given by God.
biblical_def: “Out of the eater came forth meat, and out of the strong came forth sweetness” (Jdg 14:14). Samson's riddle turns on the lion he had torn and the swarm of bees that afterward filled its carcase with honey. The Philistines could not expound it in three days, and got the answer only by threatening his wife. Whatever is to be said of Samson's recklessness — and Scripture says a great deal — the riddle itself is a true parable of God's way: out of the thing that devours, sweetness; out of the strong, food. Joseph's brothers meant evil and God meant good; the cross was the devouring of the Son and is the bread of the world. The second use turns the noun toward mercy. God's word, Isaiah says, is like the rain and the snow, which water the earth “that it may give seed to the sower, and bread to the eater” (Isa 55:10) — two kinds of provision, one for planting and one for eating, and the word of God supplies both: it multiplies through sowers, and it feeds the hungry directly. The third is judgment: Nineveh's strongholds are fig trees with the firstripe figs, which “if they be shaken, they shall even fall into the mouth of the eater” (Nah 3:12). A fortress so ripe it drops into the mouth of whoever shakes the tree.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines eater as one who eats; that which eats or corrodes; and eat as to chew and swallow, and figuratively to consume or corrode.
webster_full: EATER, n. One who eats; that which eats or corrodes.
EAT, v.t. To bite or chew and swallow, as food.
1. To corrode; to wear away; to separate parts of a thing gradually, as by rust.
2. To consume; to waste.
scriptures: And he said unto them, Out of the eater came forth meat, and out of the strong came forth sweetness. And they could not in three days expound the riddle.

For as the rain cometh down, and the snow from heaven, and returneth not thither, but watereth the earth, and maketh it bring forth and bud, that it may give seed to the sower, and bread to the eater:
Nah 3:12
All thy strong holds shall be like fig trees with the firstripe figs: if they be shaken, they shall even fall into the mouth of the eater.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The noun is plain and its biblical uses are figurative rather than doctrinal, so no framework has needed to bend it.

The principle to recover is the shape of Samson's riddle, which is the shape of providence. Out of the eater comes meat. The believer is not promised that the lion will not meet him in the way; he is promised that God brings honey out of the carcase, and that the thing which came to devour becomes, in God's hand, the thing that feeds. Joseph said it to his brothers, Paul said it of his thorn, and the cross says it loudest. This is not a sentimental claim that suffering is secretly pleasant. The lion was real and the tearing was real. But the honey was real too, and it was found in the very place the danger had been.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'akal (H398), to eat, to devour, to consume; 'okel (H398 participle), the eater; chidah (H2420), a riddle or dark saying.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'akal (H398) — to eat, devour, consume; the participle gives the eater in all three verses.
Hebrew chidah (H2420) — a riddle, an enigma, a dark saying; Judges 14:12-19, Numbers 12:8, Psalm 78:2.
Hebrew ma'akal (H3978) — food, meat, that which is eaten; the meat that came out of the eater.
Hebrew bikkurah (H1063) — the firstripe fig, the early fruit; Nahum 3:12, ready to fall at a shake.
Greek bibrosko (G977) — to eat; John 6:13, of the fragments that remained.
usage: “Out of the eater came forth meat” — and honey in a lion's carcase.
“Bread to the eater” — the word both sows and feeds.
“Fall into the mouth of the eater” — a fortress ripe enough to drop.

pos: v. and n. (to go, to travel, to be in a condition; and the price paid for passage)
etymology: Saxon faran, to go or travel — the root still visible in wayfaring, welfare and farewell. Both biblical senses descend from it: to fare is to go on, and a fare is what you pay to be carried.
biblical_def: Jesse sends David to the camp with ten cheeses for the captain and one errand: “look how thy brethren fare, and take their pledge” (1Sa 17:18) — go and see how they do. That is the old sense of the verb: not what a man eats but how he goes on. It is the errand of an ordinary son on an ordinary morning, and it puts him in the valley when Goliath comes out. The noun is Jonah's, and it is one of the saddest details in the prophets: “he found a ship going to Tarshish: so he paid the fare thereof, and went down into it, to go with them unto Tarshish from the presence of the LORD” (Jon 1:3). Flight from God costs money. There was a ship, there was an opening, there was a price he could afford — and none of that made it providence approving his errand. Three times in the verse he goes down: down to Joppa, down into the ship, and later down into the sides of the vessel and down to the bottoms of the mountains. The last use is the ordinary courtesy at the end of the Jerusalem letter: “from which if ye keep yourselves, ye shall do well. Fare ye well” (Act 15:29) — go well, travel well, be in good case.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines fare as to go, to pass, to travel; to be in any state, good or ill; and as a noun, the price of passage, or food provided.
webster_full: FARE, v.i. To go; to pass; to move forward; to travel.
1. To be in any state, good or bad; to be attended with any circumstances or train of events, fortunate or unfortunate.
FARE, n. The price of passage, or the sum paid or due for conveying a person by land or water.
1. Food; provisions of the table.
scriptures: Jon 1:3

But Jonah rose up to flee unto Tarshish from the presence of the LORD, and went down to Joppa; and he found a ship going to Tarshish: so he paid the fare thereof, and went down into it, to go with them unto Tarshish from the presence of the LORD.
And carry these ten cheeses unto the captain of their thousand, and look how thy brethren fare, and take their pledge.
That ye abstain from meats offered to idols, and from blood, and from things strangled, and from fornication: from which if ye keep yourselves, ye shall do well. Fare ye well.
corruption_summary: An open door is treated as divine approval; Jonah found a ship, and it was sailing away from God.
corruption_paragraphs: A whole style of guidance rests on circumstance: the door opened, the ticket was available, the timing worked, therefore God must be in it. Jonah 1:3 is the standing refutation. There was a ship at Joppa going exactly where he wanted to go, and he could pay the fare, and every one of those facts was true while he was fleeing the presence of the LORD. Providence arranges the means of a rebellion as surely as the means of an obedience, and it does so without endorsing either. The revealed will of God in His word, not the alignment of circumstance, is what tells a man where he ought to be.

The other half of the picture is Jesse's errand. David was sent to see how his brothers fared and to bring back a token, and that unremarkable obedience placed him in the valley of Elah on the day Israel needed a champion. God's great turns are usually reached through small assigned duties rather than through discerned destinies. The man who wants to know God's will for his life will generally find it lying in the errand his father gave him this morning.
roots_summary: Hebrew shalom (H7965), peace, welfare, how one does; sakar (H7939), hire, wages, fare; Greek rhonnumi (G4517), to be strong — the farewell formula.
roots_lines: Hebrew shalom (H7965) — peace, soundness, welfare; 1 Samuel 17:18, literally look to the peace of thy brethren.
Hebrew sakar (H7939) — hire, wages, the price paid; Jonah 1:3, the fare of the ship.
Hebrew yarad (H3381) — to go down; used three times of Jonah's flight — down to Joppa, down into the ship, down into the sides.
Hebrew 'arubbah (H6161) — a pledge, a token; the pledge David was to bring back.
Greek rhonnumi (G4517) — to be strong, to fare well; Acts 15:29, the closing word of the Jerusalem letter.
usage: “Look how thy brethren fare” — an errand that ended in a valley.
“So he paid the fare thereof” — and the ship was real, and the flight was sin.
“Fare ye well” — the letter's last word to the Gentile churches.

pos: adj. (abundant; yielding abundance, chiefly of rain, of land and of the harvest field)
etymology: From plenty, Latin plenus, full. In the Authorized Version the word attaches to a rain, a country and a field — three gifts, and in three of the four occurrences the gift has been either defiled or taken away.
biblical_def: “Thou, O God, didst send a plentiful rain, whereby thou didst confirm thine inheritance, when it was weary” (Psa 68:9). The rain is God's, sent to a weary inheritance, and it establishes what was drooping. That is the word at its best: abundance as a confirming mercy rather than a reward. Then Jeremiah, in the LORD's own indictment: “I brought you into a plentiful country, to eat the fruit thereof and the goodness thereof; but when ye entered, ye defiled my land, and made mine heritage an abomination” (Jer 2:7). The plenty was the setting of the sin, not its remedy. A people fed on the goodness of a land they did not clear turned it to idols within a generation, which is the standing danger of every prosperous church and every comfortable household. The remaining two uses are the withdrawal. Of Moab and of the vineyards of Sibmah: “gladness is taken away, and joy out of the plentiful field… the treaders shall tread out no wine in their presses; I have made their vintage shouting to cease” (Isa 16:10); and again, “joy and gladness is taken from the plentiful field… none shall tread with shouting; their shouting shall be no shouting” (Jer 48:33). The field is still plentiful. What has gone is the singing in it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines plentiful as copious, abundant, ample; yielding abundant crops; and adds that it is applied to that which produces plenty.
webster_full: PLENTIFUL, a. Copious; abundant; adequate to every purpose; as a plentiful supply of water.
1. Yielding abundant crops; fruitful; fertile; as a plentiful year.
PLENTY, n. Abundance; copiousness; full or adequate supply.
PLENTEOUS, a. Abundant; copious; plentiful; sufficient for every purpose.
scriptures: Psa 68:9
Thou, O God, didst send a plentiful rain, whereby thou didst confirm thine inheritance, when it was weary.
Jer 2:7
And I brought you into a plentiful country, to eat the fruit thereof and the goodness thereof; but when ye entered, ye defiled my land, and made mine heritage an abomination.

And gladness is taken away, and joy out of the plentiful field; and in the vineyards there shall be no singing, neither shall there be shouting: the treaders shall tread out no wine in their presses; I have made their vintage shouting to cease.

And joy and gladness is taken from the plentiful field, and from the land of Moab; and I have caused wine to fail from the winepresses: none shall tread with shouting; their shouting shall be no shouting.
corruption_summary: Plenty is read as God's verdict on a people; Jeremiah 2:7 makes it the occasion of their apostasy.
corruption_paragraphs: The prosperity teaching treats material abundance as the visible measure of God's favour, and its quieter cousin in ordinary churches treats a full building, a healthy budget and comfortable members as evidence that God is pleased. Jeremiah 2:7 forbids the inference: I brought you into a plentiful country… but when ye entered, ye defiled my land. The plenty was genuine and it was God's gift, and it became the setting of the worst idolatry in Israel's history. Deuteronomy 8 had warned of exactly this — when thou hast eaten and art full, beware lest thou forget the LORD.

The corrective is Psalm 68:9, where the plentiful rain confirms a weary inheritance. Abundance in Scripture is given to sustain a people in their calling, not to certify their standing. And Isaiah and Jeremiah supply the final sobering note: judgment does not always empty the field. Moab's field stayed plentiful; God simply removed the shouting from the winepress. A life may keep every outward good and lose the gladness in it, and that loss is itself a judgment worth fearing.
roots_summary: Hebrew nedabah (H5071), a free-will offering — used of the plentiful rain; karmel (H3759), a fruitful field or garden-land; tob (H2898), goodness.
roots_lines: Hebrew nedabah (H5071) — a voluntary gift, a free-will offering; Psalm 68:9, a rain of liberalities — the rain itself is God's freewill offering to His people.
Hebrew karmel (H3759) — a fruitful field, garden-land, plantation; Isaiah 16:10 and Jeremiah 48:33, the plentiful field.
Hebrew tub (H2898) — goodness, the best of a thing; Jeremiah 2:7, the fruit thereof and the goodness thereof.
Hebrew hedad (H1959) — the shout of the treaders at the winepress; the sound God says He has caused to cease.
Greek polus (G4183) — much, many, plenteous; Matthew 9:37, the harvest truly is plenteous.
usage: “Thou… didst send a plentiful rain” — to confirm a weary inheritance.
“I brought you into a plentiful country… ye defiled my land”.
“Joy out of the plentiful field” — the field kept, the singing taken.

pos: n. and v. (the price paid; the charge or expense of a thing)
etymology: Latin constare, to stand at a price, through Old French coust. Scripture uses the word at exactly two places where it matters most: the price of an altar and the price of discipleship.
biblical_def: “Neither will I offer burnt offerings unto the LORD my God of that which doth cost me nothing” (2Sa 24:24). Araunah had offered the threshingfloor, the oxen for the sacrifice and the threshing instruments for wood, freely and as a king gives; and David refused, and bought it at a price. The parallel in Chronicles has him say it plainly: “I will not take that which is thine for the LORD, nor offer burnt offerings without cost” (1Ch 21:24). The place he bought is the site of the temple. Worship that costs the worshipper nothing was refused at the very ground where the house of God would stand, and the principle has never been repealed. Our Lord applies the same word to the other side of the transaction: “which of you, intending to build a tower, sitteth not down first, and counteth the cost, whether he have sufficient to finish it?” (Luk 14:28). He is not warning men away from discipleship; He is refusing to enlist anyone on false terms. The cost is stated before the invitation is accepted: hating father and mother by comparison, bearing the cross, forsaking all. And 2 Samuel 19:42 gives the mean version — Judah protesting they had eaten nothing at the king's cost, as though nearness to the king were about what could be got from him.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines cost as the price, value or equivalent of a thing purchased; expense; and figuratively, the pains or labor bestowed.
webster_full: COST, n. The price, value or equivalent of a thing purchased.
1. Expense; amount in value paid, or to be paid.
2. Loss or expense of any kind; detriment; pain; suffering.
COST, v.t. To be bought for; to require to be given or expended in barter or purchase.
scriptures: And the king said unto Araunah, Nay; but I will surely buy it of thee at a price: neither will I offer burnt offerings unto the LORD my God of that which doth cost me nothing. So David bought the threshingfloor and the oxen for fifty shekels of silver.
For which of you, intending to build a tower, sitteth not down first, and counteth the cost, whether he have sufficient to finish it?
And king David said to Ornan, Nay; but I will verily buy it for the full price: for I will not take that which is thine for the LORD, nor offer burnt offerings without cost.

And all the men of Judah answered the men of Israel, Because the king is near of kin to us: wherefore then be ye angry for this matter? have we eaten at all of the king's cost? or hath he given us any gift?
corruption_summary: The gospel is presented as costless because it is free; Scripture holds both — free to the sinner, and everything to the one who follows.
corruption_paragraphs: Two errors stand on either side of this word. The first is the easy-believism that, rightly insisting salvation is by grace alone and cannot be purchased, wrongly concludes that following Christ asks nothing — and so enlists converts who were never told what they were joining. Luke 14 is our Lord's own method, and it is the opposite of modern recruiting: He turned to great multitudes and stated the terms in their hardest form, twice telling them to sit down and count first. Grace is free; discipleship is total. Bonhoeffer's phrase for the alternative — cheap grace — names it exactly, and its fruit is a church full of people who never counted.

The second error is the reverse: making the cost the price of admission, so that a man supposes his sacrifices contribute to his acceptance. David's refusal at the threshingfloor guards against that too, for the altar he bought was a place of atonement he could not perform for himself. What he refused was an offering that cost the offerer nothing; he never imagined the fifty shekels purchased forgiveness. The right posture holds both: nothing of mine can buy it, and nothing of mine is withheld from Him who did.
roots_summary: Hebrew mechir (H4242), price, hire; chinnam (H2600), for nothing, freely; Greek dapane (G1160), expense, cost.
roots_lines: Hebrew mechir (H4242) — price, purchase money; 2 Samuel 24:24, I will surely buy it of thee at a price.
Hebrew chinnam (H2600) — gratis, for nothing, without cause; the word behind that which doth cost me nothing.
Hebrew goren (H1637) — a threshingfloor; the place bought, and the site of the temple (2Ch 3:1).
Greek dapane (G1160) — expense, cost; Luke 14:28, counteth the cost.
Greek psephizo (G5585) — to count with pebbles, to calculate; the deliberate reckoning our Lord requires before enlistment.
usage: “Of that which doth cost me nothing” — refused, on the temple ground.
“Sitteth not down first, and counteth the cost” — our Lord's own method with a crowd.
“Have we eaten at all of the king's cost?” — nearness reckoned as profit.

pos: n. (the act of selling; the transfer of a thing for a price)
etymology: Saxon sala, from sellan, to give or deliver. In the Authorized Version the noun belongs almost entirely to the law of jubile, where every sale in Israel was provisional and every price was calculated by the years remaining.
biblical_def: Israel's land law made a sale into something closer to a lease. “Then let him count the years of the sale thereof, and restore the overplus unto the man to whom he sold it; that he may return unto his possession” (Lev 25:27). A man who had sold his inheritance under hardship, or a kinsman acting for him, could redeem it by reckoning the years and repaying the balance. The price itself was set by the calendar: “the price of his sale shall be according unto the number of years, according to the time of an hired servant shall it be with him” (Lev 25:50). Nothing in Israel was sold outright, because the land was not ultimately the seller's — the land shall not be sold for ever: for the land is mine (Lev 25:23). Every deed in the nation carried an expiry, and every fiftieth year returned families to their fields. That is the economic shape of the doctrine of stewardship, and it is the soil out of which the word redemption grows: a kinsman with the right and the means, paying a reckoned price to restore a man to his possession. Deuteronomy adds the Levite's exception: he may minister and eat like portions “beside that which cometh of the sale of his patrimony” (Deu 18:8), his private inheritance not counted against his portion at the altar.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines sale as the act of selling; the exchange of a commodity for money of equivalent value; and notes that a thing is on sale when offered to buyers.
webster_full: SALE, n. The act of selling; the exchange of a commodity for money or its equivalent.
1. Vent; power of selling; market.
2. Public auction; a sale of goods to the highest bidder.
REDEEM, v.t. To purchase back; to ransom; to liberate or rescue from captivity or bondage by paying a price.
scriptures: Then let him count the years of the sale thereof, and restore the overplus unto the man to whom he sold it; that he may return unto his possession.

And he shall reckon with him that bought him from the year that he was sold to him unto the year of jubile: and the price of his sale shall be according unto the number of years, according to the time of an hired servant shall it be with him.
Deu 18:8
They shall have like portions to eat, beside that which cometh of the sale of his patrimony.
corruption_summary: Absolute ownership is assumed as the natural state of property; Leviticus 25 makes every sale in Israel provisional under a divine title.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern property thinking begins from absolute private title: what a man buys is his without remainder, and what he sells is gone without recall. Leviticus 25 begins somewhere else — the land is mine; for ye are strangers and sojourners with me — and every sale in Israel was therefore a transfer of the harvests remaining until jubile, priced by the calendar. This is not a warrant for the modern collectivist reading that has been laid over these chapters; the jubile does not abolish property but protects it, returning families to their own inheritance and preventing the permanent accumulation of land in a few hands. It is a divine title above human titles, not the abolition of human titles.

The principle to recover is that redemption is a property word before it is a devotional one. A kinsman with the right, the willingness and the price restores a man to his possession — and that is exactly what Boaz did for Naomi's field and Ruth, and exactly what Christ has done for His people. Ye are bought with a price (1Co 6:20). The reckoning of years in Leviticus 25:50 is the shadow; the blood of the Lamb is the price that never needed recalculating.
roots_summary: Hebrew mimkar (H4465), a sale, that which is sold; ga'al (H1350), to redeem as a kinsman; yobel (H3104), jubile.
roots_lines: Hebrew mimkar (H4465) — a sale, merchandise, that which is sold; Leviticus 25:27, 25:50, Deuteronomy 18:8.
Hebrew ga'al (H1350) — to redeem, to act as kinsman-redeemer; the verb that makes a sale reversible.
Hebrew yobel (H3104) — the jubile, the ram's-horn year; every fiftieth year, when possessions returned.
Hebrew 'achuzzah (H272) — a possession, a holding; the inheritance a man returns to.
Greek agorazo (G59) — to buy in the market place; 1 Corinthians 6:20, Revelation 5:9, thou hast redeemed us to God by thy blood.
usage: “Let him count the years of the sale thereof” — every price set by the calendar.
“The price of his sale shall be according unto the number of years”.
“The sale of his patrimony” — the Levite's own, beside his portion at the altar.

pos: n. (concord; a compact or bargain between parties)
etymology: From agree, Old French agreer, to receive with favour. In the Authorized Version the noun names three bargains: one offered by an Assyrian, one made with death, and one that Paul says cannot exist at all.
biblical_def: Rabshakeh stood before the wall of Jerusalem and made the most reasonable offer in the Old Testament: “Make an agreement with me by a present, and come out to me, and then eat ye every man of his own vine, and every one of his fig tree, and drink ye every one the waters of his cistern” (2Ki 18:31). Vine, fig tree and cistern — he offers Israel her own covenant blessings in exchange for surrender, which is how the tempter always words it. Isaiah records the same speech (Isa 36:16) and elsewhere names the bargain the scoffing rulers of Jerusalem had actually made: “We have made a covenant with death, and with hell are we at agreement… for we have made lies our refuge” (Isa 28:15). Men do make agreements with death; they simply do not use the phrase. And God's answer is flat: “your covenant with death shall be disannulled, and your agreement with hell shall not stand” (Isa 28:18). Then Paul, drawing the line for the church: “what agreement hath the temple of God with idols? for ye are the temple of the living God” (2Co 6:16). The question is rhetorical because the answer is none. There are matters on which the people of God may agree with the world and matters on which agreement is itself the apostasy.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines agreement as concord, harmony, conformity; union of opinions; and a contract or bargain, the stipulation of parties.
webster_full: AGREEMENT, n. Concord; harmony; conformity.
1. Union of opinions or sentiments; as, a good agreement subsists among the members.
2. Resemblance; conformity; similitude.
3. Contract; bargain; compact; the stipulation of parties, or the writing containing it.
scriptures: And what agreement hath the temple of God with idols? for ye are the temple of the living God; as God hath said, I will dwell in them, and walk in them; and I will be their God, and they shall be my people.

Because ye have said, We have made a covenant with death, and with hell are we at agreement; when the overflowing scourge shall pass through, it shall not come unto us: for we have made lies our refuge, and under falsehood have we hid ourselves:
And your covenant with death shall be disannulled, and your agreement with hell shall not stand; when the overflowing scourge shall pass through, then ye shall be trodden down by it.

Hearken not to Hezekiah: for thus saith the king of Assyria, Make an agreement with me by a present, and come out to me, and then eat ye every man of his own vine, and every one of his fig tree, and drink ye every one the waters of his cistern:
corruption_summary: Agreement has been elevated to a virtue in itself; Scripture asks first what is agreed to, and with whom.
corruption_paragraphs: The reigning instinct is that agreement is good and disagreement is a failure of charity, so that the church's highest duty becomes finding common ground. Paul's question in 2 Corinthians 6:16 destroys the premise. Between the temple of God and idols there is no agreement to be found, and the search for one is not charity but treason. This is the ground on which the Reformation stood: Rome and the Reformers were not two parties in need of a settlement but a corruption and a recovery, and the men who died at Smithfield died rather than sign an agreement that would have cost them nothing but their confession.

The subtler warning is Isaiah 28:15. Nobody in Jerusalem announced a covenant with death; they made prudent arrangements and told themselves the overflowing scourge would pass over. That is how such agreements are always made — not at an altar to Molech but in a council chamber, in the language of realism, with lies as a refuge and falsehood as a hiding place. God's reply is that the agreement will not stand. Every arrangement a man makes to be safe apart from Christ is annulled on the day it is tested.
roots_summary: Hebrew chozeh (H2374 sense of a seer's compact), an agreement or vision-pact; berakah (H1293), a blessing — the Assyrian idiom; Greek sumphonesis (G4783), concord, harmony of sound.
roots_lines: Hebrew chazuth (H2380) — an agreement, a compact, literally a vision or thing seen; Isaiah 28:15, 28:18, the agreement with hell.
Hebrew berakah (H1293) — a blessing; 2 Kings 18:31 literally reads make with me a blessing — surrender dressed as benediction.
Hebrew berith (H1285) — covenant; the covenant with death set beside the agreement with hell.
Greek sumphonesis (G4783) — concord, agreement, symphony; 2 Corinthians 6:15-16, in a chain of five such questions.
Greek eidolon (G1497) — an idol, an image; that with which the temple of God has no agreement.
usage: “What agreement hath the temple of God with idols?” — and the answer is none.
“With hell are we at agreement” — nobody says it that way at the time.
“Make an agreement with me by a present” — your own vine, for your surrender.

pos: n. (a gathering of money for a sacred purpose; the contribution of a congregation)
etymology: Latin colligere, to gather together. The Authorized Version uses it twice of the temple tax Moses laid upon Israel and once of Paul's relief fund for the poor saints at Jerusalem — giving both the maintenance of worship and the care of the poor a settled, ordered channel.
biblical_def: The word appears three times and covers the whole of Christian giving. Twice it is the temple money: Joash rebukes the high priest — “Why hast thou not required of the Levites to bring in out of Judah and out of Jerusalem the collection, according to the commandment of Moses the servant of the LORD… for the tabernacle of witness?” (2Ch 24:6) — and then a proclamation goes through Judah and Jerusalem “to bring in to the LORD the collection that Moses the servant of God laid upon Israel in the wilderness” (2Ch 24:9). Note that reformation here consists in resuming a duty the law had already established; the king does not invent a scheme, he restores a lapsed one. The third is Paul's: “Now concerning the collection for the saints, as I have given order to the churches of Galatia, even so do ye” (1Co 16:1). What follows is the New Testament's only detailed instruction on the mechanics of giving: upon the first day of the week, every one of you, lay by him in store, as God hath prospered him, that there be no gatherings when I come. Weekly, individual, proportionate, laid aside in advance, and handled by men the churches themselves chose and sent — Paul was careful to provide things honest in the sight of all men. Giving in Scripture is neither spontaneous emotion nor pressure applied in the moment; it is a settled practice, ordered like the rest of worship.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines collection as the act of gathering; that which is gathered; and specifically, a gathering of money in a religious assembly for charitable or pious purposes.
webster_full: COLLECTION, n. The act of collecting or gathering.
1. The body formed by gathering; an assemblage; as a collection of men.
2. A contribution; a sum collected for a charitable purpose. Now concerning the collection for the saints. 1 Corinthians 16.
3. A gathering, as of matter in an abscess.
scriptures: Now concerning the collection for the saints, as I have given order to the churches of Galatia, even so do ye.

And the king called for Jehoiada the chief, and said unto him, Why hast thou not required of the Levites to bring in out of Judah and out of Jerusalem the collection, according to the commandment of Moses the servant of the LORD, and of the congregation of Israel, for the tabernacle of witness?
And they made a proclamation through Judah and Jerusalem, to bring in to the LORD the collection that Moses the servant of God laid upon Israel in the wilderness.
corruption_summary: Giving is worked by pressure and appeal; Paul makes it weekly, proportionate, laid aside beforehand and openly accounted.
corruption_paragraphs: The fundraising instinct of modern religious broadcasting — the urgent need, the seed-faith promise, the emotional appeal at the highest point of a meeting — is precisely what 1 Corinthians 16:2 was designed to prevent: that there be no gatherings when I come. Paul wanted the money already laid by, decided in advance and in private, so that no man's giving would be the product of the pressure of a moment. Every one of you, upon the first day of the week, as God hath prospered him. Weekly rather than occasional; individual rather than institutional; proportionate rather than flat; deliberate rather than impulsive.

The second safeguard is accountability, and it is Paul's own. He would not carry the collection alone: the churches chose men to travel with him, avoiding this, that no man should blame us in this abundance which is administered by us: providing for honest things, not only in the sight of the Lord, but also in the sight of men (2Co 8:20-21). An apostle submitted his handling of other people's money to independent witnesses. Any ministry that resists the same scrutiny has departed from the apostolic pattern at the exact point where the pattern is most explicit.
roots_summary: Hebrew mas'eth (H4864), a tribute or contribution lifted up; Greek logeia (G3048), a collection or gathering of money; thesaurizo (G2343), to lay up in store.
roots_lines: Hebrew mas'eth (H4864) — that which is lifted up, a tribute, a contribution; 2 Chronicles 24:6, 24:9, the collection Moses laid upon Israel.
Greek logeia (G3048) — a collection, a gathering of money; 1 Corinthians 16:1-2, the only two occurrences in the New Testament.
Greek thesaurizo (G2343) — to lay up, to store; 1 Corinthians 16:2, lay by him in store.
Greek euodoo (G2137) — to prosper, to have a good journey; 1 Corinthians 16:2, as God hath prospered him — the measure of the gift.
Greek diakonia (G1248) — ministry, service; 2 Corinthians 8-9, Paul's standing name for the relief fund itself.
usage: “Concerning the collection for the saints” — and then the mechanics, in detail.
“The collection… for the tabernacle of witness” — reformation as a resumed duty.
“That there be no gatherings when I come” — decided beforehand, in private.
